course.title: Small intestine
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Part of GI tract between stomach and colon → pyloric valve → Bauhin ileocecal valve
  • Length = 5-6 m
  • Duodenum (D1-D4; between pylorus and angle of Treitz)
  • Jejunum – proximal 2/5
  • Ileum – distal 3/5
  • Duodenum = retroperitoneal organ; anterior covered by serosa, posterior only adventitia
  • Jejunum and Ileum can´t be differentiated from the outside → only internal structure is different
  • Ileum: lumen narrows, vascular arches become more irregular, circular folds of mucosa shorten and become rarer,

Peyer’s plaques

The mesentery

  • Reflection of posterior parietal peritoneum → form visceral peritoneum on bowl loops
  • Fixes small bowel to posterior wall of abdomen
  • Contains fatty tissue, mesenteric vessels, lymphatic nodes and nerves
  • posteriorly – 10-20 cm, oblique from left side of L2 to right sacroiliac joint
  • anteriorly – free part 5-6 m, represents the insertion of the jejunum and ileum

Arteries, veins, lymph, innervation

Arterial supply- Jejunal and ileal arteries derive from upper mesenteric artery
- Antemesenteric margin is less vascularized → ischemic small bowel occur
here fist
Venous drainage- Upper mesenteric vein = consecutive branch of portal vein
Lymph vessels- Start with central chyliferous vessel → go through mucosa, submucosa and
subserosa, then lymph nodes in mesentery
- From here lymph reaches intestinal trunk and Pequet’s cistern
Nervous innervation- Parasympathetic innervation → right vagus
- Sympathetic innervation → great and small splanchnic nerves
- Intestinal pain being mediated only by afferent sympathetic nerves

Intestinal layers and cells

Serosa- Visceral peritoneum
MuscularisMuscularis- Auerbach plexus
- Internal circular and external longitudinal
Submucosa= most mechanical resistant sheath
- Containing nerves (Meissner plexus) + vessels
Mucosa- Muscularis mucosae, Kerckring valves, Villi, Crypts, Brunner/ Lieberkühn glands
- Peyer’s patches

Intestinal epithelium contains 4 cell types

Cylindrical cells- Achieve absorption
Calceiform cells- Secrete mucus (mature cell form)
Paneth cells
Entero-endocrine cells= Argetaffins, enterochromaffins

Physiology

  • Digestion and absorption
  • All ingested food, fluid and secretions from stomach, liver, pancreas reach small bowel
  • Total volume 9 l/ 24 h → 7 l will be absorbed; 1-2 l follow on tract to colon for further processing

2 types of small bowel contractions

Segmentation contraction- Mixes chyme with digestive juices and puts it into contact with
absorption surface
- Moving it slowly downwards
Peristaltic contraction- Is a wave moving on 10-15 cm, and then disappears
- Strong peristaltic waves going full length are not physiological in humans

Digestion and absorption

Starch- Starts with salivary amylase, completed by pancreatic amylase at duodenal/ upper
jejunal level
- Whole bowl can absorb monosaccharides → finished at level of upper jejunum
Cellulose= Not digestible
- Form fibers important in increasing fecal mass and avoiding constipation
Proteins- Digested mainly due to trypsin
Lipids- Digested due to pancreatic lipase, bile acids (→ forming micelles)
Vit. B12 and
other
vitamins		- Forming complex with intrinsic factor from stomach → decomposed at ileum cells
→ penetrating cells through pinocynosis/ combined with transporter
- Folic acid, thiamine, ascorbic acid → absorbed by active mechanism
- Hydrosoluble vit. diffuse passively through mucosa
- Fat-soluble vit. are dissolved by formation of micelles (→ bile!) → absence of bile
prevents their absorption, with exception of vit. A

Malformations of the small bowel

  • Classified according to Duhamel and Hagel
1. Development abnormalities- All manifest in form of occlusion
→ Agenesia = usually fatal
→ Atresia = neonatal surgery, risk of malnutrition by loss of an
important intestinal segment
→ Stenosis = may stay asymptomatic for long time
→ Duplications = mostly in ileum, tubular or cystic
→ Abnormal persistence of embryonic elements = complete or
partial persistence of omphalo-mesenteric canal
(complete → elimination of gas/ meconium/ ileal content through
pinpoint orifice at umbilical level)
→ Meckel’s diverticulum = derived from limited fibrosis between the
umbilicus and omphalomesenteric canal (vitellin duct)
2. Position, rotation, joining abnormalitiesa) Total absence of rotation
b) Partial absence of rotation
c) Malrotation or inverse rotations (situs inversus)
3. Abnormalities by extrinsic compression
(ring pancreas)
4. Histological structure abnormalities
(related to nerves and epithelia)

Small bowel diverticuli

  • Uncommon
  • Increases with age >70
  • Males more affected
  • Usually asymptomatic, incidentalomas
  • Classification - congenital (rare)/ acquired
Primary acquiredCongenital
- False diverticula = no muscular wall, only from
herniation of mucosa and submucosa through
muscular layer
- Frequently associated with colon diverticulosis
- Abnormalities of myenteric plexus with motor
dysfunctions		- True diverticula = full thickness of wall
- Often limited to duodenum and ileum
- Duodenal diverticula: usual incidental finding,
often located within 2 cm of papilla of Vater (area
of weakening)
- Merkel´s diverticulum

Signs and symptoms

  • 80% are asymptomatic
  • Non-specific symptoms
  • Colicative pain/ cramps, localized periumbilical, after meal
  • Gain loss
  • Malabsorption syndrome (anemia, Vit. B12 def., hypoproteinemia)

Diagnosis

  • Esogastroduodenoscopy (limited to duodenum)
  • Colonoscopy with last cm of ileum
  • CT
  • Small bowel fluoroscopy with barium contrast (irigography)
  • Capsule endoscopy
  • Enteroscopy (can visualize jejunum and ileum)

Treatment

Conservative- NSAIDs, antibiotics
Surgical- In case of complications
- Small bowel segmentary resection with entero-enterostomy

Complications

  • Acute inflammation → diverticulitis
  • Hemorrhage
  • Occlusion
  • Malabsorption

Meckel’s diverticulum

  • Most frequently congenital malformation of GI tract
  • True diverticulum
  • Persistence of omphalomesenteric canal from intrauterine life
  • Appears like a cul de sac 1-12 cm long, open on antimesenteric side of small bowel
  • In 90% located in last 60 cm of ileum; in 10% connection between tip of diverticulum and post. surface of umbilicus
  • Contains its own blood pedicle
  • May have ectopic tissue
  • 80% gastric mucosa
  • Pancreatic tissue
  • Duodenal/ colonic/ jejunal mucosa

Signs and symptoms

  • Mostly asymptomatic → becomes symptomatic through complications
  • Acute diverticulitis
  • Intermittent abdominal pain
  • Anorexia, vomiting
  • Fever
  • Leukocytosis, neutrophilia
  • May mimic acute appendicitis (DD !!!!) → check last 80-100 cm of ileum when performing an appendectomy

Complications

  • GI bleeding (hematochezia/ melena and anemia) – most common in children (other causes have to be ruled out)
  • Diverticular peptic ulcer (heterotopic gastric mucosa)
  • Diverticulitis → perforation → peritonitis
  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception/ enterolites)
  • Incarceration → Littre inguinal hernia
  • Carcinogenesis → adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis

  • Enteroclysis
  • Intestinal fluoroscopy
  • Endoscopic capsule
  • CT (blind end, inflamed structure in mid abdominal cavity)
  • Atechnetium-99mTc (identifies gastric mucosa; inverstigation of choice in children)

Treatment (surgical)

  • In case of complications → emergency (peritonitis, occlusion, bleeding)
  • If bleeding is occult, causing anemia but no other symptoms → barium enema prior to surgery !
  • Antisecretory or H2 receptors blocker in ulcers
  • Symptomatic diverticulum needs to be removed
  • Laparoscopic resection
  • Small bowel wedge resection = diverticulectomy or segmentary enterectomy with entero-enterostomy

Acquired diverticuli

  • Macroscopically = sack-like cavities (false diverticula)
  • Usually diverticuli are multiple and decrease in frequency from Treitz’s ligament to ileocecal-valve
  • Becoming symptomatic mostly > 60 years
  • Most common complication → bleeding, perforation; rarely malabsorption
  • Therapy of choice = segmental resection of small intestine

Crohn’s disease

= chronic, transmural inflammatory process of bowel characterized by abdominal pain, diarrhea and extraintestinal s.

  • High risk of complications (fistulas, abscesses (intra-abdominal or anoperineal), intestinal occlusion)
  • Affects any part of GI tract from mouth to anus, highest incidence in terminal ileum
  • Granulomas (similar to tuberculous)
  • Evolves in active bouts

Epidemiology and etiology

  • Ethnic factor: Jewish people followed by Caucasians
  • Age-sex: Two incidence peaks – 3rd decade (15-35 years) and 6th decade of life, females
  • Genetic factor: HLA-B27
  • Geographical factor: developed countries, disease incidence increased constantly in last 40 years
  • Idiopathic (cause unknown)
  • Infections, psychosomatic, environmental (smokers), nutrition (ingestion of food antigens), immunological
  • Smoking – increases risk 3 folds
  • Relationship between gut mucosa – gut bacteria deranged → T cells in intestinal lamina propria overreact to

contact with certain antigens → uncontrolled intestinal inflammation

Pathology

Macroscopic- 50% ileo-colic, 30% colon, 30% small bowel, 2% gastric or duodenal
- Thickened intestinal wall and mesentery
- Enlarged lymph nodes
- Multiple, deep, longitudinal, curvy and transversal ulcers
- Cobblestone mucosa with edema and hyperemia
→ intestinal loops will stick together forming bundles → fistulas, abscesses
- Parts of normal mucosa (discontinous)
- Affects all the layers (transmural) → fibrosis forms stenosis → occlusion
Microscopic- Transmural ulcers; aphthous
- Loss of layering, submucosal edema of villi
- Rich lymph plasma infiltrate → causing thickening
- Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells

Signs and symptoms

  • Acute abdominal pain !
  • RUQ → involvement of terminal ileum
  • Food ingestion often triggers pain → weight loss → growth retardation in children, delayed puberty/ menstruation;

rarely due to malabsorption

  • Stenosis → obstruction → colics
  • Diarrhea ! with pathological fluids (mucus, blood, pus (→ skin patches)
    • a) Incomplete recovery of bile salts (osmotic diarrhea) → cholestyramine treatment (binds bile salts)
    • b) Bacterial infection → tetracycline, metronidazole
    • c) Fistulas → esp. duodeno-/ jejuno-colic; shunting whole intestinal absorption surface → diarrhea due to

undigested bolus reaching colon; only solution = surgery

  • d) Extensive colon involvement in inflammatory process → mucosal destruction → sulphosalazine, corticoids
  • Ano-perineal or perineal suppuration
  • Abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting
  • Intermittent, low-grade fever
  • Tender mass in right iliac fossa
  • Secondary anemia due to occult bleeding, rarely hematochezia → pallor, fatigue

Extraintestinal manifestations

  • Joint disorders: ¼ of cases, coincide with active phases, large joint (frequently knee), ankylosing spondilitis
  • Skin lesions: erythema nodosum, gangrenous pyodermitis during active phases
  • Eye disorders: uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, episcleritis; associated with spondylitis
  • Intraabdominal fistulas and abscesses: entero-colic/ entero-vesical/ entero-enteric/ entero-cutaneous/ recto-vaginal/ ano-perineal, intestinal perforations of ulcerations are not free but rather inside bundles or blocks built by adhesions → intestinal abscesses; high recurrence
  • Bile lithiasis: alteration of bile composition, interruption of entero hepatic cycle, secondary to advanced terminal ileitis or surgical removal (only side to reabsorb bile salts), decrease of bile salts concentration
    • “lithogenic bile”
  • Renal lithiasis (oxalic): secondary to injuries to terminal ileum or surgical removal, deficient reabsorption of free fatty acids that will “bind” endoluminal calcium,
  • Risk of malignancy: after long evolution (18-20 years), adenocarcinoma, 70% involve terminal ileum; prognosis more severe (diagnosis is delayed → symptomatology masked by primary disease and endoscopic access often impossible duet o stenosis); usually multiple (synchronous), located on ceco-ascending portion

Complications (exam !!!)

IntestinalSystemicPost-OP
- Strictures → bowel obstruction
- Fistula
- Perforation → peritonitis
- Intraabdominal and perianal abscess
- Mesenteric lymphadenopathy
- Neoplasm		- Arthritis
- Ankylosing spondylitis
- Sclerosing episcleritis
- Uveitis
- Sclerosing cholangitis
- Oxalate stones (renal)
- Bile lithiasis (↓ bile salts)
- Erythema nodosum
- Pyoderma gangrenosum		- Early complications
- Recurrences at other intestinal segments
- Anastomotic fibrostenosis
- Adhesional obstruction
- Fistulas
- Dehiscence of intestinal sutures

Positive diagnosis

  • No specific symptoms → late
Patient history- Body weight loss
- Recurrent digestive compliants (pain, diarrhea)
- History of anemia
- Fever of unknown cause
- Undeveloped stature in children
- Positive family history
Physical exam- Pallor
- Weight loss
- Inflammatory tumor in right iliac fossa
- Peri-anorectal fistulas or abscesses
- Extraintestinal manifestations (fever, anemia, joint pain)
Lab analysis- Anemia by iron deficiency
- Hypoalbuminemia
- Increased ESR
Paraclinical tests- Barium enema/ irigography (segmental, stenosis of terminal ileum, fistulas, damaged
intestinal segments alternating with healthy ones (cobblestone aspect)
- Endoscopy/ enteroscopy
- Colonoscopy (normal lower colon and rectum or evidence of complications, early
aphtoid ulcerations with normal surrounding mucosa, later extensive ulcers,
edematous mucosa, cobblestone, stenoses)
- CT (intestinal stenosis, wall thickening, interileal abscesses, DD with intestinal
tuberculosis, lymphoma, ilio cecal tumours)
Histology- Confirms diagnosis

DD

  • Mainly UC !!!
  • Intestinal TBC (pulmonary signs, bacillus history)

Treatment

  • Maintaining remission of disease
  • Control of symptoms
  • No curative treatment available
Conservative
Etiological
Symptomatology		- Lifestyle changes
- Amino salicylates (Sulfasalazine, Mesalazine) !
- Corticosteroids (Prednisone, Methylprednisolone) !
- Immunosuppressive drugs (Azathioprine, Methotrexate, Mercaptopurine) only if both above fail
- Biologic agents anti-TNF (Infliximab, Adalimumab)
- Antibiotics
- Loperamide for diarrhea
- Anemia → iron, vit. B12, folic acid
- Malnutrition → calories supplements; parenteral nutrition
- Eye, skin, joint disturbances → corticosteroids, NSAID’s
Surgical- Surgeries are emergencies or elective
- In case of complications: stenosis/ obstruction, fistulas/ perforations, abscesses, neoplasia
- In case of failure of medical therapy
1) Intestinal stenosis/ obstruction → depending on size, duration
→ Right hemicolectomy + ileo-colic anastomosis or ileostomy
→ Ileo-colic or ceco-ileal excision + anastomosis of ileal stump to cecum/ ascending colon or
ileo transverostomy/ ileostomy
→ Jejuno-ileal segmental resection + entero-enteric anastomosis
→ Internal bypass of super and substenotic segments
→ Stricturoplasty
  • 2) Fistula → perforation
  • Internal f. a. Ileo-cecal or ileo-ileal: rarely require surgery, only with abscesses → limited ileo-cecal or ileo-colic resection + end-end or end-side anastomosis b. Ileo-sigmoid: most frequent, ileo-cecal or -colic and sigmoid resection + anastomoses c. Ileo-colic: total colectomy + ileostomy d. Ileo-vesical: frequent; hematuria, pneumaturia, fecaluria, pyuria, pollakiuria; ileal segment resection + anastomosis e. Recto-vesicle, colo-vesicle f. Ileo-vaginal, recto-vaginal, colo-vaginal g. Colo-jejunal, colo-gastric and colo-duodenal
  • External f.: spontaneous, very rare, at anastomotic sutures, often require reoperation, drainage

of peri-fistular abscess, late fistulas occur with new active bout

  • Free perforation into peritoneal cavity → colostomy, Hartmann resection
  • 3) Intraabdominal/ hepatic abscess → drainage or by US/CT guided puncture
  • 4) Hemorrhage → rarely massive
  • 5) Toxic megacolon (more common in UC)
  • X ray → empty abdomen with gas column of >5 cm + leukocytosis, tachycardia, >38°C
  • Subtotal colectomy with ileostomy
  • Antibiotics
  • 6) Fulminant colitis has the same therapeutic management which, applied in time, improves and

eventually cures toxemia

  • Diarrhea after removal of ileum (over 1 m) subsides with cholestiramine

Entero-mesenteric infarction (= EMI)

= abrupt and persistent suppression of blood flow in main trunk/ branches of upper/ lower mesenteric arteries/ veins or even capillary microcirculation → hemorrhagic necrosis of involved intestinal segment

Epidemiology

  • Age > 50y

Classification and etiology

I. EMI of arterial trunk origin→ 60%
A. Embolic
B. Thrombotic (37%)
C. Other causes
II. EMI of venous trunk origin→ 40%
- Only thrombotic
III. Obstruction in partial→ 20%
microcirculation

A. Mesenteric artery embolism

  • From left ventricle or atrium, rarely paradoxical embolism (shunt from right to left)
  • Favoring diseases → MV disease, HF, acute MI, subacute bact. endocarditis, AF (most common, 80%)
  • Thrombo-embolic (61%), athero-embolic

B. Mesenteric artery thrombosis

  • > 50 y → atheromas → art. HTN, blood stasis (MI, HF)
  • < 40 y → inflammatory Buerger’s thromboangiitis, periarteritis nodosa

C. Other causes

  • Aortic dissection
  • Closed abdominal trauma

Pathogenesis

  • Suppression of blood flow in tributary to obstructed vessel
  • Embolus causes strong reflex arterial spasm both above and below
  • Causes secondary extensive postembolic thrombosis above and below site of injury
  • Arterial EMI - mostly by upper mesenteric artery (90%) and only 10% due to lower mesenteric artery
    • SMA has sharp angle when branching from aorta, lower one has wider, arch like, angle
  • Venous EMI - 96% in upper mesenteric vein, history of pelvic or lower caval phlebitis, hypercoagulation (polycythemia, hemoconcentration, post splenectomy thrombocytosis), venous stasis (portal hypertension, extrinsic tumoral compression on portal vein), suppurative processes (peritonitis, colic diverticulitis), abdominal trauma, irradiation, surgery
  • EMI → ischemia → necrosis → perforation and septic endotoxic shock (bacterial load of intestine, massive increase of microbial flora in ischemic and distended small bowel → endo and exotoxins that penetrated
  • Hypovolemic due to rapid massive accumulation of plasma and blood cells in intestinal wall thickness and lumen

Pathomorphology

  • Infarction develops in 3 stages
1. Apoplexy- Characterized by plegic dilation, secondary to prolonged spasm, of capillary
circulation, with intraparietal plasma exudates (cyanotic, edematous red
loop)
- Potentially reversible
2. Infarction proper- In which capillary effractions occur, allowing blood flooding of lumen and
intestinal wall (true intraluminal and intraparietal hemorrhage), intraparietal
hematoma is constituted, loop being purplish-black
3. Gangrenous stage- Loop appears greenish-gray, limp, presenting multiple perforations
- Stercoral peritonitis
  • Lesions might be segmental or extended, clearly deliniated

Clinically

  • Onset brutal, with signs of acute abdomen, continue to aggravate
  • Altered general state
  • Pallor, sweaty, restlessness with cold extremities, marbled skin → state of intense shock (low Bp, high HR)
  • Abdominal pain is very severe, violent and persistent, maximal intensity in peri-umbilical area
  • Distended abdomen, intestinal transit for feces and gas is absent (obstipation)
  • Diarrhea with enterorrhagia appears later
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Can be preceded by “abdominal angina” (intermittent, reversible attacks of mesenteric ischemia during meals)

Physical exam

  • Abdominal distention, painful to palpation, maximal at affected loop, which is sometimes felt as a soft sausage
  • Signs of peritoneal irrigation appear rapidly, generalized muscle contraction (peritonitis)
  • Percussion → tympanism (distension and dullness due to peritoneal fluid)
  • Auscultation → “deadly silence” (absence of peristalsis)
  • DRE → rounding and sensitivity of Douglas’s pouch, bloody stool

Paraclinical exam

  • Lab → leukocytosis (> 15.000), low Hb and Hct, low K, metabolic acidosis, hyperazotemia, hyperamylasemia
  • X-ray of empty GI tract → marked aerocolia (selective angiography of upper mesenteric a.)
  • Abdominal US → dilation of loops above, ischemic loops with thickened walls, without peristalsis, peritoneal fluid
  • Doppler US → may detect level of obstacle and even differentiate between thrombosis and embolism

DD

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Intestinal occlusion
  • Ruptured extrauterine pregnancy
  • Posterior MI

Prognosis

  • Mortality 80-93%

Treatment

  • Quick metabolic rebalancing → volemic and acid-base restoration with at least 2 i.v. lines
  • CVP monitoring
  • Blood transfusion
  • Nasogastric aspiration
  • Antibiotics
  • Peridural infiltration - advantages: analgesia, to fight shock, improvement of microcirculation of non-ischemic

intestine; contraindication: collapse (aggravates hypotension)

Intraoperative decision making depends on

  • Condition of intestine
  • Assessment of mesenteric vascularization
  • Presence or absence of peritonitis

In incipient infarction with injuries considered potentially reversible and vascular trunk obstacle, vascular procedures are required, such as:

  • a) Embolectomy
  • b) Thrombendarteriectomy followed by venous or synthetic patch
  • c) Re-implantation of mesenteric artery into aorta
  • d) Aorto-mesenteric bypass
  • These procedures must be initiated within first 6-8 h
  • Drug therapy in early stages: anticoagulants, antiplatelet, vasodilators, streptokinase
  • After 12-36 h → 2nd laparotomy to look for possible irreversible lesions → enterectomy of necrotic loops + washing

and drainage of peritoneal cavity

  • Diffuse ischemia doesn’t require resection → mesenteric arterial catheter
  • In extended lesions at advanced stages any surgical intervention is useless
  • Venous thrombosis is solved with difficulty and uncertainty
  • Portal vein thrombosis contraindicates intestinal resection → BUT if intestinal injury is reversible → direct portal

thrombectomy may be performed with anticoagulation therapy

Results

  • Embolectomy → 60% mortality
  • Thrombendarteriectomy → 80% mortality
  • Venous thrombectomy → 95% mortality
  • Resection without vascular procedures → 60-95% mortality

Tumors of the small intestine

  • Represent 1-5% of GI tract neoplasms
  • Mainly benign
  • Frequency from less to most affected: duodenum → proximal jejunum → terminal ileum
  • > 45 years
  • Asymptomatic (only 10% symptomatic) → symptoms mainly caused by malignant lesions (hemorrhage, occlusion,

intussusception)

  • Low incidence explained by
    • fast movement of nutrients (short time contact with mucosa)
    • Liquid consistency of intestinal chyme
    • Alkaline pH
    • High levels of benzilperoxidase, IgA
    • Lymphoid tissue (solitary lymphoid nodules/ Peyer’spatches)

Risk factors

  • Familial adenomatous polyposis
  • Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC or Lynch syndrome)
  • Celiac disease
  • Heavily salted food
  • Smoking
  • Alcohol consumption
  • Often synchronous tumors (primary one in colon)

A. Benign neoplasms

Polyps/ adenomas- Have malignant potential in time
- Adenomatous or villous
- Often solitary
- Manifested by bleeding or occlusion by invagination/ intussusception
GIST= gastrointestinal stromal tumors
- Originating in interstitial Cajal cells
- Malignant potential
- Extraluminal growth, highly vascularized → bleeding
- Hematogenous metastasis
- Treatment: Imatinib (Gleevec); surgical resection
Juvenile polyps or retention
polyps		- May complicate with hemorrhage or occlusion by invagination
- They occur more frequently in colon
- May be eliminated spontaneously by self-amputation before adolescence
Endometriosis
Leiomyomas, schwannomas,- May become symptomatic by hemorrhage or occlusion, acute abdomen
representing surgical indication
lipomas, hemangiomas
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
→ Polypoid hamartomas		Peutz-Jeghers syndrome- Solitary in patients without associated lesions
- Usually multiple in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome = diffuse polyposis of whole GI
tract and hyperpigmentation of mucosa and around orifice
- Very low malignancy potential
- Surgery for symptomatic cases and when polyps > 1 cm must be removed
→ Polypoid hamartomas
Gardener’s syndrome/ FAP= characterized by familial polyposis located to colon and small intestine,
associated with osteomas and fibromas or subcutaneous sebaceous cysts
- Premalignant lesion after age of 40
- Increased incidence of duodenal periampullar cancers

B. Malignant neoplasms

Adenocarcinoma= most frequent primary tumor
- Usually affects proximal jejunum or distal ileum
- Asymptomatic → 80% have metastases when diagnosed
- Produces intestinal occlusion
- Late lymphatic dissemination and metastases
- Segmental resection with adjacent mesentery, adenopathies involving upper
mesenteric artery may create problems
- Survival after 2 years is 25%
Lymphoma- With ileal starting point infiltrates submucosa and transforms affected
portion into rigid segment
- 1/3 of patients present malabsorption syndrome
- Wide segmental resection + splenectomy, retroperitoneal ganglia biopsy and
liver biopsy for staging
Leiomyosarcoma- Frequently in children and young adults
- Tend to ulcerate and bleed
- Jejunum
- 50% due to malignant melanoma metastases
- Other cancers with metastases in small bowel = cervical, renal, pulmonary
- Surgery in patients with good general condition
Carcinoid tumors- Originate in endocrine cells in intestine
- Secretory or non-secretory (benign)
- Associate with neoplasms of other enterochromaffin tissues (medullary
thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma)
- Age group: 25-45 years
- Ranks 2nd place after appendix
- Usually in ileum
- Macroscopic: firm, yellowish nodules situated under mucosa
- Slow evolving tumor, but fast metastasizing
- Asymptomatic, diagnosed often with l.n. or liver metastasis
- Can cause pain, bleeding, occlusion or carcinoid syndrome (flushed skin,
diarrhea, bronchial constriction assoc. with right heart valve disorders)
- Serotonin, histamine, catecholamines, bradykinin, kalikrein, prostaglandins,
ACTH and calcitonin
- Elevated serum serotonin and urinary 5-HIA
Treatment
- Segmentary enterectomy + lymphadenectomy
- Whipple procedure for duodenal tumors
- Right hemicolectomy for distal ileum
Secondary tumors (metastasis)- Primary tumor: uterus, ovaries, stomach and malignant melanoma
- Hematogenous metastasis
- Poor prognosis

Signs and symptoms

  • Diffuse abdominal tenderness
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Hemorrhage – occult/ melena/ hematochezia
  • Anemia
  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception) – König syndrome (alternating diarrhea and constipation)
  • Palpable mass (late diagnosis)

Complications

  • Intestinal obstruction (volvulus/ intussusception)
  • GI hemorrhage - occult (anemia)/ acute (melena/ hematochezia)
  • Perforation → peritonitis

Diagnosis

  • Barium enema, enteroclysis
  • Enteroscopy, endoscopic capsule
  • Abdominal ultrasonography: tumors > 4cm
  • CT scan: >2 cm
  • Selective arteriography, Angio CT
  • Exploratory laparoscopy

The small intestine Benign disorders of the small bowel

Ion Cosmin Puia

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY

The small bowel or small intestine is about 5 m long, from Treitz’s angle to Bauhin’s iliocecal valve. The upper two fifths form the jejunum, and the lower three fifths the ileum. There is no clear limit between the jejunum and the ileum, though as it nears the iliocecal valve the lumen narrows, vascular arches become more irregular, the circular folds of the mucosa shorten and become rarer, while Peyer’s plaques (submucosal lymphatic tissue patches) are more frequent in the ileum. The jejunum occupies more the left side of the peritoneal cavity, the ileum occupies the hypogastrium and the right iliac fossa.

The small bowel is fixed to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery, a reflection of the posterior parietal peritoneum. The insertion base goes from the left of the median line downwards and obliquely to the right to the right iliac fossa. The mesentery sheets continue on the small bowel in the form of visceral peritoneum.

The mesentery contains arteries, veins, lymph vessels and nodes, and nerves. The jejunal and ileal arteries derive from the upper mesenteric artery, it forms two arches of 2-3 generations from which short vessels derive and go ti the intestine on the mesenteric margin. The antemesenteric margin is less vascularized, ischemic small bowel alterations first occurring at this level. Venous drainage is ensured by the upper mesenteric vein, a consecutive branch of the portal vein. Lymp vessels start with the central chyliferous vessel of the villosity which continues with the mucosa, submucosa intramuscularis and subserosa, then through the lymph nodes in the mesentery. From here the lymph reaches the intestinal trunk and Pequet’s cistern.

Parasympathetic innervation is realized by fibers from the right vagus, the sympathetic one derives from the great and small splanchnic nerves. Both types have afferent and efferent branches, intestinal pain being mediated only by the afferent sympathetic nerves.

The intestinal wall is formed of 4 sheaths: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa.

Macroscopically the absorption surface of the mucosa increases by the circular folds called Kerkring’s valves, longer and more numerous in the jejunal segment/ The folds surface is extended by the villi, 1 mm long, containing an arteriole, a venules, a central canal and muscular fibers originating in the muscularis and conferring the contraction capacity. Villi are covered by a simple cylindrical epithelium with microvilli, of 1 micron. The total surface of the small intestine may increase to 200-500 sq. meters. The small intestine epithelium includes 4 cell types. Cylindrical cells achieve absorption and have a short life of 5-6 days. Mature calceiform cells are secreting mucus. Paneth cells are only found in the Lieberkuhn crypts and their function is not elucidated. The secretions of the entero-endocrine cells (argetaffins, enterochromaffins) have a complex role in the small bowel activity.

The submucosa is a fibro-elastic layer containing vessels and nerves. This is the most mechanically resistant sheath conferring strength to intestinal suture. The smooth musculature is internal circular and external longitudinal. The serosa envelops the intestine.

There are two types of contractions at the levels of the small bowel. The segmentation contraction mixes the chymewith the digestive juices and puts it into contact with the absorption surface, moving it slowly downwards. The peristaltic contraction is a wave moving at 1 cm/second on 10-15 cm, and then disappears. Strong peristaltic waves going the full length of the intestine are not physiological in humans.

The intestinal muscular activity is regulated by the nervous and humoral systems. Gastric, cholecystokinin and motilin stimulate motility, while secretin inhibits it. Encephalins, pentapeptides of the endorphin family, slow the passage. Parasympathetic fibers initiate contraction, especially in the proximal segment of the small bowel, while sympathetic impulses have an inhibitory effect.

Exogenous supply of fluids, saliva, bile, pancreatic and intestinal juices total 6-9 l, of which the small bowel absorbs a fair amount, only 1-2 l reaching the colon. Water and electrolytes change is achieved by absorption and secretion and is influenced by polypeptide hormones, neurotransmitters, prostaglandins and certain bacterial toxins.

Starch digestion starts with the action of salivary amylase and is completed by the pancreatic amylase at the level of the duodenum and upper jejunum. Hydrolysis products are decomposed into monosaccharides under the action of enzymes in the cylindrical epithelium. Though the whole bowel can absorb monosacchariced, this is practically finished at the level of the upper jejunum. Cellulose and semicellulose, together with lignine, are not digestible by the human enzymes and form the fibers so important in increasing the fecal mass and avoiding constipation.

Proteins are digested mainly under the action of tripsin, while 80% of the amminoacids absorption is achieved in the first 100 cm of the jejunum. Lipids are decomposed by pancreatic lipase, though bile acids play an important role, forming micelles. Conjugated bile acids form micelles in lower concentrations than the unconjugated ones. Therefore their deconjugation under bacterial action, such as in the blind loop syndrome, leads to decreased lipid absorption. Conjugated bile acids are absorbed in the lower ileum and are returned by portal route to the liver, where they are secreted again into the bile. Ileum disorders or extensive resection break this cycle and considerable amounts of bile acids go to the colon where they determine water and electrolytes secretion causing diarrhea. The same effect is given by fatty acids remained in the intestinal lumen due to malabsorption.

Due to its large molecule, vitamin B12 has a special absorption mechanism. It combines with the intrinsic factor (Castle), a mucoprotein secreted by the gastric wall cells. The complex is decomposed at the surface of the ileum cells, and vitamin B12 penetrates the cells through pinocinosis or combined with a transporter (transcobalamides). Folic acid, thiamine and ascorbic acid are also absorbed by active transport. Other hidrosoluble vitamins diffuse passively through the mucosa. Liposoluble vitamins are dissolved by formation of micelles and absorbed like any other lipid. The absence of bile prevents their absorption, with the exception of vitamin A.

MALFORMATIONS OF THE SMALL BOWEL

Malformations of the small bowel may be classified according to Duhamel and haegel into:

1. Development abnormalities

2. Position, rotation, joining abnormalities

3. Abnormalities by extrinsic compression (ring pancreas)

4. Histological structure abnormalities (related to nerves and epithelia).

Development abnormalities include agenesia, atresia, stenosis. They manifest in the form of occlusions. Agenesias are usually fatal. Atresias benefit from neonatal surgery, which entails the risk of malnutrition because of the loss of an important intestinal segment. Stenoses may stay asymptomatic for a long time or they may be discovered by chance.

Duplications, also considered developmental abnormalities, affect mostly the ileum. Cystic duplicates are more frequent than tubular ones.

Abnormal persistence of embryonic elements includes the complete or partial persistence of the omphalo-mesenteric canal. Complete persistence is manifested clinically by elimination of gas, meconium or ileal content through a pinpoint orifice at the umbilical level. Fistulography evidences the communication with the intestine. The umbilical opening without intestinal communication leads to the appearance of umbilical polyp or sinus, which appears as a granuloma or a canal variable in length requiring resection. Meckel’s diverticulum is derived from the limited fibrosis on the segment between the umbilicus and the omphalomesenteric canal.

Rotation abnormalities include total absence of rotation (associated with a common mesentery), partial absence of rotation, malrotation or inverse rotations (associated with situs inversus).

SMALL BOWEL DIVERTICULI

MECKEL’S DIVERTICULUM is present in 2% of the population and is the most common congenital anomaly of the digestive tract. It is due to the persistence of the omphalomesenteric canal from the intrauterine life. It appears like a cul de sac 1 – 12 cm long, open on the anti-mesenteric side of the small bowel. In 90% of the cases it is situated in the last 60 cm of the ileum. In 10% of the cases the connection between the tip of the diverticulum and the posterior surface of the umbilicus is kept through a fibrous cord.

Meckel’s diverticulum is a true one, i.e. it contains all the layers of the small intestine. The ectopic tissue is found in 50% of symptomatic Meckel’s d. Gastric mucosa with parietal cells occurs in 80% of these cases. The pancreatic tissue or the duodenal, colic or jejunal types of mucosa are more rarely encountered.

Meckel’s d. becomes symptomatic through complications only in 4% of the patients, 50% of them being children under the age of 10, 80% young people under 30.

Bleeding occurs in 25% of the patients with symptomatic Meckel’s diverticulum, at the level of the heterotopic gastric mucosa. It is the most frequent cause of digestive hemorrhage in children, more frequent before the age of 2 years.

Intestinal occlusion represents 30% of Meckel’s d. complications. It may occur through volvulus around the diverticulum fixed to the wall, by its invagination or by involving an intestinal loop under the adhesion formed by the diverticulum.

Acute diverticulitis occurs more rarely due to the usually large base. Secondarily, stenoses may occur at the level of the diverticular neck, intestinal content stasis leading to diveritculitis manifested by abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever and high leukocyte count. Objective examination evidences signs similar to acute appendicitis, from which diverticulitis is difficult to differentiate preoperatively.

Perforation may be secondary to diverticulitis and occurs when the inflammation processed has been triggered.

Ulcer on the ectopic mucosa may manifest as chronic abdominal pain.

Paraclinical examinations may outline the positive diagnosis. Barium enema or enteroenema may evidence the diverticulum. Tc99 scintigraphy is useful if in the diverticular wall there is ectopic gastric mucosa.

Differential diagnosis should be established according the complication. Hemorrhage from the diverticulum should be considered after ruling out other bleeding source by endoscopy. The obstructive form requires emergency surgery, as there are no signs to show the exact nature of the occlusion. Diverticulitis is often confounded with appendicitis, with or without perforation. Common surgical indication makes delaying it both useless and dangerous. Therefore it is wise to check the last 80-100 cm of ileum when performing appendicectomy.

Surgical indication is absolute and urgent when it evolves towards peritonitis, occlusion or profuse bleeding. If bleeding is occult, causing anemia but no other symptoms, surgery may be delayed in order to further investigate by Ba enema, enetro-enema etc. Antisecretory or H2 receptors blocker medication may be of help in the case of bleeding from an ulcer on ectopic gastric mucosa.

The symptomatic diverticulum must be removed. The wedge resection is recommended in order to make sure all ectopic or scarring tissues are removed, or even segmental intestine resection. Operation may be laparoscopic or by applying a linear stapler at the diverticulum base.

Prognosis of the disturbances related to Meckel’s d. is good. However, due to late diagnosis and late surgery, mortality remains at 6%.

ACQUIRED DIVERTICULI

Congenital diverticuli, except Meckel’s, are rare, but the acquired or false ones occur in 1.3% of radiographic or necrotic studies. Macroscopically they are sack-like cavities 1-2.2 cm diameter, with a wide neck and wall formed only of mucosa and submucosa. They herniated through the vascular penetration orifices in the intestinal wall, on the mesenteric margin and penetrate through the mesentery sheets. Usually diverticuli are multiple and decrease in frequency from Treitz’s ligament to the ileocecal valve, becoming symptomatic mostly after the age of 60. The association with colic or duodenal diverticulosis is found in 30% of cases.

The most common complications are bleeding and perforation. Rarely, in patients with numerous diverticuli, a malabsorption syndrome may occur through a mechanism similar to the blind loop. Barium enema or enteroenema evidence diverticuli.

Choice therapy is segmental resection of the small bowel.

CROHN’S DISEASE

Crohn’s disease was first described by Crohn, Ginzburg and Oppenheimer at Mont Sinai Hospital, New York in 1932, as a chronic disease characterized by abdominal pain, diarrhea and extraintestinal symptoms. Evolution is associated with complications such as fistulas, abscesses (intra-abdominal or ano-perineal), as well as intestinal occlusion.

Morphopathologically the disease affects the terminal ileum, though it may involve the whole GI tract.

Microscopically, granulomas similar to the tuberculous ones appear in the affected structures.

EPIDEMIOLOGY

1. Ethnic factor: the disease was found mostly in Jewish people,

especially the ones in Western Europe and the United States.

Caucasian race is more affected than the black race.

2. Age-sex:the onset is mainly between 15-35 years, females being more

affected.

3. Genetic factor: there is undoubtedly a genetic predisposition for

Crohn’s disease, the risk being directly correlated with the closeness

of the relation. On the other hand, 40-50% of the monozygous twins

will be both affected, while the risk is 1 /26 for heterozygous twins.

4. Geographical factor: there are geographical areas more affected by

Crohn’s disease, namely developed countries (Western Europe,

Scandinavia, United States of America), as compared to other areas

(Asia, Africa, South America), where the disease is more rare.

To be noted that the disease incidence increased constantly in the last 40 years.

ETIOPATHOLOGY

The cause of Crohn’s disease is unknown.

A number of factors have been incriminated, which generated various theories trying to explain the etiology. Among them: infections, psychosomatic, environmental (it is unanimously accepted that smokers have a 3-4 times higher risk), nutrition (ingestion of food antigens), immunological (h=genetic predisposition of T cells in the intestinal lamina propria to overreact to the contact with certain antigens). All these theories seem to complete rather than exclude one another.

It is possible that Crohn’s disease should occur due to an immune disturbance genetically determined; in this context, food and/or infectious antigens may trigger an exaggerated immune response, which entails chronic inflammation.

PATHOMORPHOLOGY

The most frequent location is ileo-colic (40-50%). In 30% of cases only the colon is affected; the small bowel as sole site occurs in 30% of the cases, the gastric or duodenal only 1-2%. In fact, any location on the GI tract is possible.

Fig.22: Complete ileal stenosis (arrow)

Macroscopically the mesentery of the diseased segment is much thickened, tending to include its serosal lymph nodes are enlarged. A longitudinal section evidences thickened intestinal wall. The endoluminal surface is full of multiple, longitudinal, curvy and transversal ulcers, their crisscrossing giving the aspect of cobblestone of the oedematous mucosa that protrudes through them. The characteristic of Crohn’s disease is that it affects all the intestinal wall layers; the fibrosation in time of the lesions generates stenoses (the morphopathological basis of the occlusive complications). Also, the intestinal loops will stick together forming bundles, fixed adhesive blocks within which fistulas (entero-enteral, entero-colic, colo-colic) will create communications, pathological shunts (duodeno- or jejuno-colic ones may cause severe malabsorption and malnutrition syndromes); interintestinal abscesses caused by these passages in the walls are also present.

What is important is that affected intestinal segments alternate with normal segments.

Microscopically: rich lymph-plasma infiltrate involves all the intestinal wall layers causing its thickening. Aphtous ulcerations are found over lymphoid follicles, as well as noncaseous granulomas containing giant cells.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

Abdominal pain and diarrhea are the most common manifestations, but others may include: ano-perineal or perineal suppuration, hematochezia, extraintestinal symptoms (arthritis, cutaneous lesions, stomatitis, eye disturbances), and systemic manifestations (fever, weight loss, small stature and late sexual maturation in children).

1.Abdominal pain is frequent, diverse in character, depending on the type of lesion and pathogenetic mechanism generating it. For the primary physician it is important to interpret this correctly, as it will lead to an adequate management of the disease. Thus, in patients with intestinal stenoses in place, pain may have a sudden onset, with typical colics once the occlusive complication occurs and in association with other cardinal signs, especially in patients without any history of weight loss, anemia, or altered ESR. In such cases, pain is caused by the occlusion (the complication), not by Crohn’s disease; correct management is not to administer corticosteroids. Nasogastric aspiration will usually resolve these episodes. In case of recurrence at shorter or one-two months intervals, surgery will remove the stenosed intestinal segment.

During Crohn’s disease evolution, the clinical picture (and management) differs. The onset is slow, not sudden, often preceded by a weight loss period (due to avoidance of food ingesting); hypoalbuminemia, anemia and increased ESR are also present. In these cases corticosteroid therapy comes first.

Food ingestion often triggers pain. Increased intestinal peristalsis during and after meals will determine a clinical picture of relative stenosis (most frequently on the terminal ileum), which is silent during meals. Pain, located round the belly button – typical of small bowel – but also at the level of the right iliac fossa, accompanied by abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, will generate the patient’s reflex to give up eating, eventually resulting in body weight loss. The pain substrate is intestinal stenosis; in the active phases of the disease, it will be reversible (generated by oedema and intestinal wall inflammation) and will subside to anti-inflammatories (corticoids); in case of fibrous organic stenoses, the primary role belongs to the surgeon.

2.Diarrhea – may have various pathogenetic origins, which will lead to correct management if correctly interpreted. One of the mechanisms is:

a)The incomplete (or absent) recovery of bile salts in the terminal ileum

(made unfunctional by the disease or excised) – open entero-hepatic

circuit! – means they enter the colon, where they inhibit resorbtion and

stimulate water and electrolytes secretion (osmotic diarrhea); responds

to cholestiramine (3x4 g a day), which “binds” the bile salts. In enteral

lesions longer than 1 m, statorrhea will be so important that a diet poor

in lipids is imposed.

b)Bacterial infestation of the small bowel (especially above the

entero-colic fistulas) will respond to antibiotics: tetracycline,

metronidazole.

c)Fistulas, especially duodeno- or jejuno-colic, shunting the whole

intestinal absorption surface, will cause diarrhea due to undigested

bolus reaching the colon. Surgery is the only solution.

d)Extensive colon involvement in the inflammatory process will cause

structural damage to the mucosa (as well as other wall structures) of

the colon, whose resorptive-retrieval function of water and electrolytes

will be abolished. In this case, antiinflammatories (sulphosalazine,

corticoids) will treat diarrhea.

3.Weight loss associated to somatic growth retardation is often found in pediatric pathology. In the adult it is generated by the fear to eat, since feeding causes pain. More rarely weight loss is caused by amalabsorption(except cases with a history of extensive intestinal resection – the surgical short bowel syndrome).

4.Anemia by iron deficiency develops slowly and progresses due to occult bleeding. Sometimes lower digestive hemorrhage is clinically manifest, the source being the ulcerations at the level of the cecum-ascending colon.

EVOLUTION varies with different degrees of severity and morbidity, often not influenced by drug therapy. Chronic, progressive evolution with active bouts is typical. Organic intestinal stenoses occur after about 8 years of evolution, determining occlusive syndromes and then mechanical obstruction which, together with fistulas and abscesses, will require surgical cure (about 80% of the patients. Another feature of Crohn’s evolution is postoperative: it will involve early complications (fistulas and dehiscence of intestinal sutures, as well as late ones (recurrence of the disease on previously untouched intestinal segments).

EXTRAINTESTINAL MANIFESTATIONS

Joint disorders are found in about a quarter of the cases and coincide with active phases. Most often one large joint is affected (frequently the knee). More rarely ankylosing spondilitis or sacro-ileitis may occur.

Skin lesions, erythema nodosum and gangrenous pyodermitis occur after small trauma, associated with active phases.

Eye disorders are uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, episcleritis associated more frequently with spondylitis or sacroileitis, as well as HLA-B27.

Intraabdominal fistulas and abscesses are characteristic for the clinical evolution of Crohn’s disease, the most frequent being entero-enteral. Intestinal perforations (of ulcerations) are not free in the peritoneal cavity but rather inside bundles or blocks built by adhesions, resulting in blocked confined intestinal abscesses which may develop into fistulas into the peritoneum, urinary bladder (entero-vesical fistulas with pneumaturia), vagina (recto-vaginal fistulas).

Entero-cutaneous fistulas (especially at the level of postoperative scars) occur after the resection of diseased segments, at the level of anastomoses, representing another characteristic feature of the disease.

Ano-perineal fistulas and abscesses are very frequent, associated with colo-rectal involvement; they may even constitute the first signs of disease. Their evolution is slow, with a tendency to recur after operation.

Bile lithiasis occurs in one third of Crohn patients and is caused by the alteration of the bile composition. Everything starts from the interruption of the entero-hepatic cycle, secondary to advanced terminal ileitis or surgical removal of this portion (known to be the only one to reabsorb bile salts), decrease of bile salts concentration in relation to cholesterol in the biliary fluid will determine “lithogenic bile”.

Renal lithiasis (oxalic usually) is secondary to severe injuries to the terminal ileum or surgical removal of this segment. The metabolic consequence is deficient reabsorption of free fatty acids that will “bind” endoluminal calcium. The natrium oxalate resulted from the absence of calcium in the bowel (“stolen” by fatty acids) is soluble and will be absorbed from the colon, determining chronic hyperoxalemia. The outcome is the onset of renal lithiasis.

Ureteral stenosis, the most frequently on the right ureter, are caused by the involvement in the sclerotic-inflammatory process near the terminal ileum and ceco-ascending colon, and may lead to hydronephrosis. Usually associated with active phases, therefore subsiding after anti-inflammatory therapy.

Crohn’s disease and the risk of malignancy; after a long evolution in time (18-20 years), Crohn disease patients risk to develop adenocarcinoma, enteral or colic, 5-7 time more often than normal population. 70% of enteral adenocarcinomas involve the terminal ileum; their prognosis is more severe in Crohn disease than for primary cancers, mainly because diagnosis is delayed by two factors: symptomatology is masked by the primary disease, and the endoscopic access to the stenosed terminal ileum is often impossible. Secondary colic adenocarcinomas are usually multiple (synchronous), located on the ceco-ascending portion and associated (preceded) bysevere mucosal dysplasia.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS

Since there are no specific manifestations of Crohn’s disease, diagnosis is generally late, years after the first signs.

I. Patient history:

1.Abdominal pain

2.Body weight loss

3.Diarrhea, anemia

4.Fever of unknown cause

5.Underdveloped stature in children

6.Positive family history

II. Physical examination:

1.Palor

2.Weight loss

3.Inflammatory tumour in the right iliac fossa

4.Peri-anorectal fistulas – abscesses

5.Extraintestinal manifestations

III. Laboratory tests:

1.Anemia by iron deficiency

2. Hypoalbuminemia

3.Increased ESR

IV. Paraclinical tests:

1.Barium enema

2.Irigography

3.Colonoscopy

V. Histological confirmation

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Children with impaired development, adolescents with delayed onset of sexual characteristics (pubic, facial or armpit hair), late onset of menstrual periods in girls, are factors that may raise the suspicion of Crohn’s disease (as all other extraintestinal symptoms: fever, anemia joint pain), even in the absence of gastrointestinal symptoms.

The tumoral mass in the right iliac fossa (often painful) should prompt for further paraclinical examinations and looking for other signs (abscesses, peri-anorectal fistulas or recurring digestive complaints).

RADIOLOGICAL EXAMINATION

Irigography, especially when the barium content is refluxed into the ileum, as well as barium passage with compression at the level of the terminal ileum reveal classical elements of radiological semeiology: segmental, rigid stenosis of the terminal ileum, fistulous entero-enteral, entero-colictrajectory trajectories, damaged intestinal segments alternating with healthy ones (cobblestone aspect).

CT scan may also evidence intestinal stenosis, wall thickening, interileal abscesses.

Radiological differential diagnosis is with intestinal tuberculosis, lymphoma, and ilio-cecal tumours.

Endoscopy is performed only in case of uncertainty and is not a routine procedure.

Colonoscopy evidences (unlike in ulcerative colitis) normal lower colon and rectum. Aphtoid ulcerations occur initially in the affected segments, discrete and with normal surrounding mucosa. Later extensive ulcers appear, linear, longitudinal, transversal; oedematous mucosa is preeminent and delimited by these ulcers, creating the cobblestone aspect. At more severe stages stenoses may appear that prevent the advancement of the colonoscope.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS is mainly with ulcerative colitis and intestinal tuberculosis (bacillus history, pulmonary signs are absent in Crohn’s disease, while antituberculous therapy is inefficient).

TREATMENT

Drug therapy

Sulphosalazine (3-4 g/day initially, then 2g/day long term)

Corticosteroids are effective in the active phases, with prompt effect on pain, diarrhea, weight loss and lab tests. Prednisolone doses are according to individual tolerance, 0.25-0.75 mg/kg.

Immunosuppressants are not recommended as first treatment due to adverse effects. They are indicated in cases in which salazopirine or corticosteroids failed, or when the latter cannot be reduced enough for long term treatment. Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) or mercaptopurine (1.5 mg/kg), cyclosporine.

Treatment of symptoms: loperaminde (2mg) is effective for diarrhea. Diarrhea induced by surgical removal of the ileum (over 1 m) subsides after cholestiramine (4g). Diarrhea by bacterial infection is treated by tetracycline.

Anemia is treated by iron replacement, vitamin B12, folic acid.

Malnutrition and physical retardation in children may be treated by calories supplements or total parenteral nutrition in severe cases.

Eye, skin and joint disturbances respond to corticoids and NSAIDS.

Surgical treatment

There are two major surgical indication categories in Crohn’s disease: emergency indications requiring intervention on sight or shortly after (high mortality), or elective surgery indications, well planned and with the intestine adequately prepared (small mortality).

In case of intestinal stenosis, depending on the size of lesions, the patient’s condition and the duration of occlusion, the surgeon may opt for a large right hemicolectomy (at ileum level), finalized by anastomosis of the ileal stump to the transversal colon; another variant, more modern, is limited ileo-colic or ceco-ileal exeresis and reimplantation of the ileal stump to the cecum or ascending colon. In long-term occlusion and altered patient condition, circumventing the ileo-cecal obstruction may be achieved by ileo-transverostomy or ileostomy.

In the particular case of patients in good condition but short surgical intestine (previous multiple jejuno-ileal resections), internal bypass is recommended (anastomosis of the super- and substenotic segments), or stricture plasty (similar to pyloroplasty), consisting of the longitudinal incision and transversal suture of the incision to the level of the stenosed area.

In perforating complications:

a)Internal fistulas

-ileo-cecal or ileo-ileal fistulas shunt small segments and rarely end up on the operative table, only when they are associated with abscesses; in these cases, a limited ileo-cecal or ileo-colic resection followed by end-to-end or end-to-side anastomosis of the stumps is sufficient.

-ileo-sigmoid fistulas are the most frequent. The solution consists of ileo-cecal (or colic) and sigmoid resection, with two anastomoses, or, if the sigmoid is less affected, the right ileo-colic resection is completed with the simple suture of the sigmoid wall defect. In case the whole colon is involved, total colectomy with ileostomy is necessary.

-ileo-vesical fistulas are also frequent and cause very unpleasant manifestations: hematuria, pneumaturia, fecluria, piuria, polakiuria. Surgery, after separation of the two organs, consists of the ileal segment resection and suture on two planes of the vesical defect, protected by uretrovesical tube kept in place for at least 7 days.

-recto-vaginal fistulas, in case of less rectal involvement,require local excision of the fibrous-sclerous, periulcerous and fistulatingtissue, with separate closure of the vaginal and rectal defect, plus an upper protective colostomy.

-colo-vaginal fistulas are rare and raise difficult problems as they require segmental, subtotal or total colectomy, depending on the extension of Crohn’s disease.

-colo-vesical fistulas are resolved by excising the colic segment in question, with or without protective colostomy.

-colo-jejunal fistulas may be generated by jejunal or colon involvement in Crohn’s disease. It generates malabsoption syndromes, diarrhea and severe weight loss. Surgery will remove both portions involved.

-colo-gastric and colo-duodenal fistulas are always originating in the colon. Excision of the effected colic segment and suture of the gastric or duodenal wall defect is the solution. For the duodenum, the simple suture may cause stenosis;therefore, the duodenal defect may be covered by a jejunal patch or even a Roux duodenal-jejunal anastomosis.

b)External fistulas: the spontaneous ones are very rare. Most external fistulas occur early, at the level of anastomotic sutures, complicating postoperative course; spontaneous cure is rare, most often it require reoperation, drainage of the perifistular abscess and external derivation above.

Late fistulas occur with a new active bout and require resection of the fistulous trajectory and excision of the affected segment.

c)Free perforation into the peritoneal cavity requires either suture with protective colostomy above, or a Hartmann resection in case of recto-sigmoid location. Abundant washing and correct drainage of the peritoneal cavity are mandatory.

d)Intra-abdominal abscesses are surgically cured. After cure, drainage and biological recovery of the patient, the fistula trajectory and the responsible intestinal segment may be resected.

e)Hepatic abscess may be treated by US-guided or CT-guided puncture. Surgery seems more radical, as it allows concomitant treatment of entero-colic lesions.

f)Hemorrhage is rarely massive (1-2%). Even if it is not massive it may be sufficient to impose excision of the segment in question. Two aspects are worth mentioning: intraoperative enteroscopy or colonoscopy or even opening the excised portion are welcome in order to establish the precise bleeding site (which sometimes may be a lesion situated far away from the most obvious macroscopic lesions).

g)Toxic megacolon, though typical of ulcerative colitis, may also occur with Crohn’s disease. the presence at the x-ray examination of the “empty” abdomen of a constant gas column of 5 cm, combined with altered general state, high leukocyte count, tachycardia and temperature over 38O Celsius impose prompt and effective treatment (corticoids, antibiotics, possible internal decompression with long tubes). Early surgery yields the best results (subtotal colectomy with ileostomy).

h)Fulminant colitis has the same therapeutic management which, applied in time, improves and eventually cures toxemia.

ENTERO-MESENTERIC INFARCTION

DEFINITION

The abrupt and persistent suppression of blood flow in the main trunk or branches of the upper or lower mesenteric arteries, mesenteric veins, or even at the level of capillary microcirculation in the intestinal wall causes hemorrhagic necrosis of the intestinal segment involved, namely entero-mesenteric infarction (EMI).

EPIDEMIOLOGY

It is generally a disorder of old ages, 80% of the cases occurring over the age of 50. Rarely, young adults or even children may be affected. Incidence has been increasing in the past 30 years, in parallel with the increasing incidence of cardiovascular diseases in general.

CLASSIFICATION

Depending on the nature of the obstacle, EMI may be:

I. EMI of arterial trunk origin (60%)

a) Embolic

  • thrombo-embolic (61%)
  • atheroembolic
  • other embolies b) Thrombotic (37%) c) Other causes II.EMI of venous trunk origin (40%) III. Obstructions in the parietal microcirculation (20%).

ETIOLOGY

A)Mesenteric artery embolismis generally due to thrombi, or, exceptionally, atheromatous content entered into circulation due to their ulceration.

The origin of the thrombi is at the level of the left ventricle or atrium, rarely in the right heart which produces the so-called paradoxical embolism due to interatrial communication with the shunt from right to left.

Diseases that favor the condition are:

* Mitral valve disease, heart failure, acute myocardial infarction,

subacute bacterial endocarditis, atrial fibrillation, closed heart surgery;

* By far the most common cause is atrial fibrillarion (80%);

* Athero-embolism originates in the atheromatous plaques;

* Other embolism, very rare, may be determined by calcareous

fragments from the aortic stenosis lesions, or mitral or aortic tissue

fragments dislodged during surgical operations on these valves;

* Also, establishing extracorporeal circulation, air bubbles may

penetrate into the systemic circulation causing embolism.

B)Acute arterial thrombosis in persons over 50 is caused by atheromas, in conditions of arterial hypotension and blood stasis (myocardial infarction, heart failure).

In patients under the age of 40, the cause of arterial embolism are inflammatory Buerger’s thromboangiitis, periarteritis nodosa).

C)Other causes

* acute dissection of the aorta may obstruct the branching out of the

upper mesenteric artery;

* closed abdominal trauma (mesentery detachment, rupture) or

abdominal wounds producing ruptures or sectioning of the

mesenteric vessels may determine EMI.

PATHOGENESIS

The main hemodynamic disturbance is suppression of the blood flow in the intestine tributary to the obstructed vessel. The embolus settled in the main arterial axis will be followed by a strong reflex arterial spasm both above and below, even at the level of the capillaries in the intestinal wall, a spasm that will close the vicious circle that will fix the embolus even more solidly. The spasm is the origin of paroxystic pain characteristic of the onset of embolism. It is followed by secondary extensive postembolic thrombosis, which represents the final blow to the intestinal wall, above and below the site of injury.

Arterial EMI are mostly due to the occlusion of the upper mesenteric artery (90%) and only 10% are due to the lower mesenteric artery, explained by the sharp angle formed by the upper mesenteric artery with the aorta, unlike the lower one, which has a wider, arch-like, angle. On the other hand, the upper mesenteric artery is a terminal type artery, while the blood flow in the lower mesenteric artery may be supplemented from the left iliac artery to which it is anastomosed by the middle hemorrhoidal arteries.

Venous EMI occurs in patients with a history of pelvic or lower caval phlebitis. The general factors favoring hypercoagulation (polycythemia, hemoconcentration, post-splenectomy thrombocytosis), or the local ones, favoring venous stasis (portal hypertension, extrinsic tumoral compression on the portal vein branches), other factors in the suppurative processes (peritonitis, colic diverticulitis), as well as abdominal trauma, irradiation, surgery, are responsible for the mesenteric vein thrombosis. 96% of them occur on the upper mesenteric vein and only 4% on the lower one.

Splenectomy represents a high risk by the postoperative thrombocytosis; when it exceeds 500,000/cubic mm, anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy is necessary to prevent mesenteric or portal thrombosis.

Besides the vascular factor, the EMI pathogenesis also includes the septic-toxic factor. Given the bacterial load of the intestine, especially the colon, the massive increase of the microbial flora in the ischemic and distended small bowel is a source of endo- and exotoxins that penetrated into the general circulation at an early stage, causing, together with vasoactive quinines (intestinal myocardial depressor and hydrolases released by the hypoxic enterocyte), endo-toxic shock.

The hypovolemic component of the shock in entero-mesenteric infarctionis due to rapid massive accumulation of plasma and blood cells in the intestinal wall thickness and lumen.

PATHOMORPHOLOGY

Infarction develops in three stages:

1. Apoplexy – characterized by the plegic dilation, secondary to prolonged spasm, of capillary circulation, with intraparietal plasma exudates (cyanotic, oedematous red loop), a stage in which the lesion is considered potentially reversible.

2. Infarction proper – in which capillary effractions occur, allowing the blood flooding of the lumen and intestinal wall (a true intraluminal and intraparietal hemorrhage), an intraparietal hematoma is constituted, the loop being purplish-black, hence compromised.

3. Gangrenous stage – the loop appear greenish-gray, limp, presenting multiple perforations. Stercoral peritonitis is in place.

According to the level of the obstacle, lesions may be segmental or extended (subtotal or total). In the total EMI, a rare form, the first 50 cm of the jejunum are usually left out.

Delimitation from the healthy areas is generally clear, the infarction area taking the shape of a triangle with the base at the level of the infracted loop and the tip to the ostium of the obstructed artery.

CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS

Symptoms are varied, depending on the extension of the injury.

The onset is brutal, with signs of acute abdomen, pain, bloating, which continue to aggravate.

EMI usually occurs in a patient over 50 years old, against an emboligenic atheromatous background (atrial fibrillation in 80% of cases).

The general state is altered from the start, the patient is pale, sweaty, restless, with cold extremities, marbled skin, in a state of intense shock and tendency to collapse (low BP with decreased differential, feeble pulse), initially normal body temperature.

Abdominal pain is very severe, violent and persistent, maximal intensity in the peri-umbilical area, it does not generally irradiate outside the abdominal region, does not respond to analgesia.

The occlusive picture is always present, the patient has a distended abdomen, intestinal transit for feces and gas is absent. Diarrhea with enterorrhagia appears later.

Nausea and vomiting are present, as a reflex at first, containing food and bile, then also blood, in the later stages.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION of the abdomen will find: abdominal distention, painful to palpation, maximal at the level of the affected loop, which is sometimes felt as a soft sausage. The signs of peritoneal irrigation appear rapidly, followed eventually by generalized muscle contraction (peritonitis).

Percussion evidences tympanism due to distension and dullness on the sides, corresponding to the peritoneal fluid. Auscultation reveals a “deadly silence”, which reflects absence of peristalsis secondary to intestinal ischemia.

Rectal touch may evidence the rounding and sensitivity of Douglas’s pouch, as well as bloody stool on the gloved finger.

PARACLINICAL EXAMINATIONS

Laboratory examinations evidence high leukocyte count (> 15,000/cubic mm), low hemoglobin and hematrocrit, low potassium, metabolic acidosis, hyperazotemia, hyperamylasemia.

X-ray of empty GI track, the patient’s condition allowing, evidences marked aerocolia, followed 6 hours later by fluid and air. Rarely a fool opaque loop with thickened walls is visualized.

Choice x-ray examination is selective arteriography of the upper mesenteric artery, which may be performed in patients with altered general state, though this is not a routine examination. It may establish the site of the obstacle. It is important in the early stages, locating the obstacle in the view of a possible revascularization.

Simple abdominal ultrasound is very useful and easy, it evidences the dilation of the loops above, the ischemic loops appearing with thickened walls, full, without peristalsis, as well as the presence of peritoneal fluid.

Doppler ultrasound is a very fine examination which may detect the level of the obstacle and even differentiate between thrombosis and embolism.

A suggestive finding is high leukocyte count in the abdominal puncture fluid 6-8 hours after arterial obstruction (Wangensteen).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS is with abdominal disorders manifested by intense pain and shock.

The first would be acute pancreatitis, the intestinal occlusion, ruptured extrauterine pregnancy, diffuse acute peritonitis by perforation of a cavitary organ (perforated ulcer etc.).

Posterior myocardial infarction may also be taken into account due to epigastric pain and shock.

EVOLUTION

It inexorably leads to death after a few hours/days if not treated. Mortality is still 80-93%.

TREATMENT

Because of the poor condition of the patient, a quick brief metabolic rebalancing is necessary in intensive care, consisting in volemic and acid-base restoration using at least two venous lines – a central vein (subclavian) is useful for CVP monitoring, blood transfusion, nasogastric aspiration, antibiotics.

Peridural infiltration has some advantages, besides analgesia (to fight shock) it somewhat improves the microcirculation of the non-ischemic intestine. It is contraindicated in case of collapse as it aggravates hypotension.

Intraoperative decision making will be based on the following:

  • the condition of the intestine
  • assessment of mesenteric vascularization
  • presence or absence of peritonitis.

In incipient infarction with injuries considered potentially reversible and vascular trunk obstacle, vascular procedures are required, such as:

a)embolectomy

b)thrombendarterectomy followed by venous or synthetic patch

c)re-implantation of the mesenteric artery into the aorta

d)aorto-mesenteric bypass

These procedures must be initiated within the first 6-8 hours of vascular obstruction and even then segmental intestinal resection is necessary, less extended though.

In the early stages of EMI by microcirculation obstruction, drug therapy includes anticoagulants, antiplatelet, vasodilators, streptokinase administered through intraarterial catheters place in the major trunk. After 12-36 hours, a second look laparotomy is performed to inspect for possible irreversible lesions.

In EMI with irreversible lesions enterectomy of the infracted necrotic loops is necessary. Small bowel or entero-colic resection must be performed no matter how mutilating, together with washing and drainage of the peritoneal cavity.

Diffuse ischemia does not require resection. Mesenteric arterial catheters may be placed in this case, with a “second look” in not too old or advanced stages patients.

In case of extended lesions at advanced stages any surgical intervention is useless.

Venous thrombosis is solved with difficulty and uncertainty.

Portal vein thrombosis contraindicates intestinal resection, but if intestinal injury is reversible, direct portal thrombectomy may be performed, with anticoagulant therapy.

Pre- intra- and postoperative balancing is essential, through peripheral and/or central venous catheters as well as intramesenteric ones, if necessary; heparin, Dextran-40, antibiotics, beta-stimulants, alpha-blockers, vasodilators (papaverin, tolasolin), and thrombolytics (streptokinase) will be administered.

RESULTS

  • embolectomy – 60% mortality
  • thromenarterectomy – 80% mortality
  • Venous thrombectomy – 95% mortality
  • resection without vascular procedures – 60-95% mortality.

BENIGN AND MALIGNANT TUMOURS

OF THE SMALL BOWEL

Ion Cosmin Puia

Small bowel tumours represent 1-5% of the GI tract tumours. The most affected is the terminal ileum followed by the proximal jejunum. 85% of the patients are over the age of 45. There is a very strong correlation between small bowel tumours and primary tumours in other locations.

Small bowel tumours become symptomatic only in 10% of the cases. Benign lesions are 10 times more frequent than malignant ones, but 75% of the symptomatic ones are malignant. Hemorrhage and occlusion, sometimes by invagination, are the most common complications.

Benign tumours

Polyps, adenomatous or villous, are much rarer in the small bowel than in the large one. They are often solitary, manifested by bleeding or occlusion by invagination.

Polypoid hamartomas may appear solitary in patients without associated lesions. In 50% of the cases hamartomas are multiple, 10% are familial with dominant autosomal transmission in the form of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome defined by diffuse polyposis of the whole GI tract and hyperpigmentation of the mucosa and around the orifice. It has very low malignancy potential. Surgery is for symptomatic cases when all polyps over 1 cm must be removed.

Gardner’s syndrome is characterized by familial polyposis located to the colon and small intestine, associated with osteomas and fibromas or subcutaneous sebaceous cysts. Colic polyps degenerate to malignancy after the age of 40. An increased incidence of duodenal periampullar cancers as found in these patients.

Juvenile polyps or retention polyps may complicate with hemorrhage or occlusion by invagination. They occur more frequently in the colon and may be eliminated spontaneously by self-amputation before adolescence.

Leiomyomas, hemangiomas, lipomas, neurofibromas or fibromas may become symptomatic by hemorrhage or occlusion, acute abdomen representing the surgical indication, while the intestinal injury is found intraoperatively.

Malignant tumors of the small bowel

Adenocarcinomais the most frequent of primary malignant tumours of the small bowel. It usually affect the proximal jejunum and remain asymptomatic for a long time, thus 80% of the patients have metastases when diagnosed. Segmental resection with the adjacent mesentery is the choice operation, though adenopathies involving the upper mesenteric artery may create problems. Survival after 2 years is 25%.

Lymphoma with ileal starting point infiltrates the submucosa and transforms the affected portion into a rigid segment. One third of the patients present a malabsorption syndrome, plus intractable fever at times. Wide segmental resection should be associated with splenectomy, retroperitoneal ganglia biopsy and liver biopsy for staging.

Leiomyosarcoma tend to ulcerate centrally and bleed secondarily.

50% of the patients with malignant melanoma have metastases. Other cancers with metastases in the small bowel are cervical, renal, pulmonary etc. Surgery is indicated in patients in good general condition.

Carcinoid tumoursoriginate in the endocrine cells in the intestine. They may associate with neoplasms of other enterochromaffin tissues (medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. The target age group is 25-45 years.

The small bowel comes second after the appendix for carcinoid tumours. The ileum is 10 times more affected than the jejunum. Tumours are multiple in 50% of the cases. Macroscopically they are firm yellowish nodules situated under the mucosa. Special stains may evidence the argirophyllic or argentaffinic nature.

Intestinal carcinoid is considered to be a slow evolving tumour. At the time of diagnosis 40% have invaded the muscularis, 33% have lymph node or liver metastases. If the primary tumour is smaller than 1 cm, only 25% have metastases, increasing to 80% if the primary node is over 2 cm. Sometimes large metastases are found originating from a small tumour.

Small tumours are usually asymptomatic. 30% of the small bowel carcinoids present with pain, bleeding occlusion or carcinoid syndrome. The latter is present in 10% of the patients, the percentage increasing in time. The clinical picture is bouts of flushed skin, diarrhea, bronchial constriction associated with right heart valve disorders. Active substances secreted by carcinoid tumours are inactivated by the liver, but liver metastases may spill these compounds directly into systemic circulation. The clinical picture is determined by a number of substances such as serotonin, histamine, catecholamines, bradykinin, kalikrein, prostaglandins, ACTH and calcitonin.

Urinary dosage of the 5-hydroiindolacetic acid is useful, though a normal value does not exclude a carcinoid tumour, as this is only a serotonin metabolite, one of the numerous mediators of the syndrome. Challenge tests are not routine yet.

Carcinoid tumours, even metastasized, have a surgical indication, sometimes repeated operations being necessary. Streptozocin is an efficient chemotherapy agent, alone or with other cytostatics.

Liver metastases may be effectively cured by selective embolization.

Treatment of symptoms is complex. Drug therapy includes phenotiazines, corticoids, H1 and H2 receptors blockers. Somatostatin is efficient for the diarrhea.

Prognosis of carcinoid tumours is relatively good. Overall survival rate after surgery is 70%. In 20-40% of the patients with metastases survival is 5 years.
